newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Pipeline UK price pressures seen flat.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Pipeline UK price pressures seen flat.

text.p: British producer prices for May, due at 0830 GMT on Monday, will show little or no sign of inflation looming on the horizon.
But that does not mean the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee acted hastily in raising rates on Friday, economists said.
The Reuters consensus forecast is for output, or factory gate prices, to have been flat last month and just 1.0 percent higher than a year earlier.
Economists said any alarm if the year-on-year rate jumped from 0.8 in April should be put to one side because output prices fell in May last year.
"Even if output price inflation has now troughed, it is unlikely to go much higher over the rest of this year," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
With the pound's relentless rise still squeezing manufacturers, any hopes manufacturers had of passing on higher prices were probably wishful thinking, he said.
If output prices are benign, input prices -- which measure what manufacturers pay for raw materials -- are lurking well in negative ground.
The Reuter poll forecast input prices rose 0.6 percent last month but that still leaves them 8.6 percent lower year-on-year.
"The combination of negative input price inflation and easing unit wage costs suggests the outlook for output price inflation remains very benign," said Philip Shaw, chief UK economist at Union Plc.
Loynes said the pound -- up about 18 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- could soon push input prices lower still.
But Shaw said that did not mean Friday's interest rate rise -- sanctioned by Britain's new-style monetary policy committee at its very first sitting -- was premature.
"Given the timing of the budget, today's decision was the correct one. A delay of a month with no concrete fiscal measures on the table would have led to serious uncertainty," he said.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will unveil his first budget on July 2. Most economists are hoping for some tax rises to take the heat out of domestic demand and reduce the need for even higher interest rates.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs agreed price pressures in manufacturing are almost entirely absent.
They said core producer prices -- excluding food, drink, tobacco and petrol -- have also fallen in the last four months months. In April, core output prices were up just 0.5 percent year-on-year.

That has yet to fully feed through to the high street, they said in a client note. "Underlying retail price inflation is comfortably set to hit the government's target of 2.5 percent or less during the second half of 1997."
However, the Bank of England and its new committee are concerned with the risks to inflation in two years' time.

"Manufacturing output...is still on a steady upward trend and with service sector activity growing more strongly than manufacturing, GDP is comfortable being maintained at an above-trend rate," the note said.
